premise: A defended enclave is a deployment pattern, not a product. This file expresses the shared-responsibility split as data so a tenant's responsibility matrix is generated from its architecture rather than transcribed from a provider's PDF. Modes are defaults for a tenant that has actually moved its CUI into the enclave; the validator re-tests every inherited assignment against the three-test rule before it will grade one.

three_test_rule.statement: An objective may be marked inherited only when all three tests pass. A failed test degrades the assignment to shared or tenant. Inheritance is never a status a tenant simply declares.

tests.test: The provider's authorization and responsibility matrix cover the objective at or above the tenant's assurance class.
The provider emits a machine-readable, signed validation for the objective within the tenant's class cadence (SIG-INHERIT-FRESH).
No tenant-side configuration, export, or endpoint re-scopes the objective back to the tenant — a tenant that pulls CUI out of the enclave has re-scoped the destination back in.

three_test_rule.note: T3 is the test tenants fail most. The enclave carries the control only for the CUI actually inside it.

enclave-only.name: Enclave-only (thin client, no local CUI landing)
enclave-only.description: All CUI processing occurs inside the enclave. Endpoints render but never store CUI; download, print, and removable media are blocked at the platform. This is the pattern with the largest scope reduction and the one most small contractors should target.

enclave-plus-endpoints.name: Enclave plus managed endpoints
enclave-plus-endpoints.description: CUI is centered in the enclave, but managed tenant endpoints process some CUI locally. Every objective that touches the endpoint returns to the tenant or becomes shared.

commercial-cloud.name: Commercial cloud and SaaS, no dedicated enclave
commercial-cloud.description: Controlled information sits in general-purpose cloud storage, SaaS applications, and tenant-managed infrastructure. The provider genuinely operates a large part of the stack, but nothing in the arrangement is scoped to controlled defense information specifically, and the provider does not emit per-tenant validation on a cadence.
commercial-cloud.inheritance_reality: A great deal is inheritable in principle and fails on evidence. A major provider really does run the datacenter, the hypervisor, and the physical media lifecycle, and no customer can or should re-perform those. What a commercial arrangement generally does not do is emit a machine-readable validation per tenant on your cadence. An annual audit report is a point-in-time artifact about the provider, not a continuous reading about your data, so most of what the provider genuinely does lands as shared rather than inherited under the three-test rule. That is a statement about evidence flow, not about whether the provider is competent.

assignments.residual: Tenant-side application and endpoint testing where the tenant runs its own code.
Tenant resilience for anything it operates outside the platform.
Provider runs platform detection; tenant owns escalation, triage, and its own response decisions.
Provider supplies platform threat intelligence; tenant applies it to its mission and supply chain.
Your people. A provider trains its own staff, never yours.
Role-based training follows the person, not the platform.
Platform baseline is inherited; tenant configuration inside its own slice is the tenant's change surface.
Provider removes unneeded platform services; tenant removes unneeded tenant services and apps.
Change review is a governance act the tenant performs over its own environment.
Provider detects platform change drift; tenant detects drift in its own configuration.
Perimeter defense is the platform's; a tenant network fronting the enclave is the tenant's.
Transit encryption inside the platform is inherited; tenant-originated paths are the tenant's.
Platform baseline immutability.
Tenant isolation is the provider's core obligation and cannot be delegated to the tenant.
Platform availability architecture.
Provider restricts platform traffic; tenant controls its own sharing, guest access, and egress settings.
Provider reviews platform perimeter; tenant reviews its own boundary declarations.
Logical network construction is platform-level.
Validated cryptography inside the enclave is inherited; CUI at rest on a tenant endpoint is the tenant's to encrypt and prove.
Marking is human judgment. The enclave supplies labeling tooling, not the decision.
Provider supplies the identity platform; the tenant owns who is in its directory.
Provider supplies phishing-resistant methods; the tenant enforces them on its own population. Capability is inherited, enforcement is not.
Least privilege over tenant roles and data is the tenant's.
Provider supplies elevation machinery; the tenant defines who may elevate.
Tenant service principals and application identities are the tenant's.
Disabling a departing employee is joined to the tenant's personnel record, which the provider cannot see.
After-action governance belongs to the contractor.
Provider contains platform incidents; the contractor runs its own incident response and owns the decisions.
The seventy-two-hour reporting obligation is the contractor's under its own contract clause and cannot be subcontracted away.
Near-eliminated when print is blocked platform-side; any printing at all returns this to the tenant in full.
Removable-media block enforced at the platform; endpoint-side control is the tenant's when endpoints exist.
Provider sanitizes decommissioned platform media; tenant sanitizes its own.
Media transport applies only where physical media exists.
Provider generates platform alerts; someone at the tenant must receive and act on them.
Platform event capture is inherited; tenant-run applications emit their own events.
Retention duration is a platform property the tenant configures within provider limits.
Continuous monitoring of the tenant's own posture stays with the tenant.
Log review is an act of attention. No provider performs it on the tenant's behalf.
Screening and separation of your people.
Datacenter physical access is inherited; the space where a person views CUI on a screen is the tenant's.
Provider escorts visitors in its facilities; the tenant escorts visitors in its own.
Provider inventories the platform; the tenant inventories what it operates and declares scope.
Executive support for security is a property of the contractor's leadership.
Security investment decisions are the contractor's.
Secure development applies to what the tenant builds.
Vulnerability disclosure is the contractor's public commitment.
Platform backup objectives; tenant data held outside the enclave is the tenant's to protect.
Platform recovery planning.
Platform recovery to stated objectives, measured by the provider's own restore tests.
Provider tests platform restore; a tenant with its own data stores tests those.
Asset categorization accuracy is the tenant's determination and the assessor's first thread to pull.
The provider publishes its matrix; the tenant proves it consumed the current one and reconciled it.
The tenant declares its own dataflow, including every path into and out of the enclave.
Provider separates tenants; the tenant separates in-scope from out-of-scope inside its own estate.
Platform supply chain, inherited through the provider's own authorization.
Provider monitors its suppliers; the tenant monitors its own subcontractors and flow-down.
Platform configuration inherited; tenant slice configuration owned.
Provider manages platform attack surface; the tenant manages what it exposes.
Storage encryption inside the platform.
Provider patches the platform; the tenant patches its endpoints and its own software.
Provider restricts platform deployment; the tenant restricts what it deploys into its slice.
With no local CUI landing the platform carries system integrity; the moment endpoints process CUI, endpoint integrity is squarely the tenant's.
Provider scans the platform; the tenant scans what it operates.
Provider remediates platform findings on its own clocks; tenant findings remain the tenant's, on the finding-queue clocks.

evidence_flow.statement: Inheritance is only real when the proof travels with the control. The provider validation feed is the mechanism.
steps: The provider runs collectors for the controls it operates and computes its own per-objective claim states, exactly as a tenant does.
It publishes a signed, machine-readable validation feed keyed by objective, carrying status, the class it sustains, the measurement timestamp, and a hash — never the underlying evidence.
The tenant ingests the feed, verifies the signature, and records provenance in its own manifest. Raw provider evidence stays with the provider; the tenant holds the attested claim and its pointer.
The tenant's validator re-runs the three-test rule on every inherited objective at ingest, and SIG-INHERIT-FRESH ages the whole inherited set together when the feed stops arriving.

The tenant's responsibility matrix, Security Decision Record, and posture rollup are then projections that already contain the inherited layer — nothing is transcribed, and a stale feed is visible as staleness rather than as silence.
evidence_flow.assessor_consequence: The assessor validates the provider's pipeline once and samples it, rather than re-walking the same inherited stack in every tenant. That single change is where population-scale assessment cost actually falls.

honest_boundary.statement: Inheritance shrinks the tenant's obligation; it never zeroes it, and this file is written so the residual is impossible to lose.
points: An unvalidated enclave inherits nothing. The provider must itself be assessed at or above the tenant's class.
The grading invariant does not relax for inherited controls: every mapped objective must still be demonstrated, by the provider rather than by nobody.
A tenant that exports CUI to an endpoint outside the enclave has re-scoped that endpoint back in, and the three-test rule will fail T3 rather than let the claim stand.
Personnel, training, marking judgment, incident reporting, governance, log review, scope declaration, and the affirmation itself never inherit.

Concentration is a real trade: enclaves reduce sprawl across thousands of under-resourced environments while increasing the consequence of one provider's failure. The framework's answer is that provider validation is continuous, machine-checked, and visible to every tenant at once — not that the trade does not exist.
